40927.etyen:
From noen (“some”) + -lunde (“manner- or degree-forming suffix”), literally “in some manner”.
The first element is from Old Norse nǫkkurn, the masculine accusative singular of nǫkkurr (“some, any”), earlier nakkvarr, from Proto-Norse. Its origin is traditionally analysed as a contraction of *ni-wait-(ek-)hwarjaʀ (“I do not know who”); reconstructions differ over whether the independent pronoun “I” was present. The negative element continues Proto-Germanic *ne (“not”), from Proto-Indo-European *né (“not”); the verbal element belongs to Proto-Germanic *witaną (“to know”), ultimately from Proto-I

6367.etyen: Inherited from Danish blegne with native Norwegian -k-, from Old Norse blikna. By surface analysis, blek (“pale”) + -ne. Traditionally pronounced /blæɪ̯nə/ in Dano-Norwegian, as still in regne, tegne etc. However, the form with a velar obstruent established itself by analogy with the underlying adjective, which did not have the same pronunciation in Norway, although it does in Denmark, cf. bleg [b̥lɑj]. (The diphthong in the forms bleik, bleikne is of different origin.)

en.g: good evening; a greeting used when meeting or taking leave of someone in the evening
x: God aften! Hyggelig å se deg igjen.
Good evening! Nice to see you again.
God aften, herr pastor! Stien er fæl –
Good evening, Reverend! The path is treacherous—

1001695.etyen:
Fixed greeting formed from god (“good”) + aften (“evening”), literally “good evening”.
The first element, god (“good”), is from Old Norse góðr (“good”), from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz (“good”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to join, unite, suit”). The second, aften (“evening”), is from Danish aften (“evening”), from Old Danish aftæn (“evening”); compare aptann (“evening”) and eptann (“evening”).
Compare the parallel greetings Danish god aften and Swedish god afton (“good evening”).

en.g: a surname originating as a patronymic, originally meaning “son of Bertel”

1001951.etyen:
From Bertel (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Bertel”. The given name Bertel is a Danish form of German Berthold, traditionally interpreted as a Germanic compound meaning “bright ruler” or “bright power”.
Compare Danish Bertelsen, Swedish Bertelson and Bertelsson (“patronymic surnames”).

1005023.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Brúarflǫt, formed from the genitive singular brúar of brú (“bridge”) and flǫt (“flat, level piece of land”), literally “bridge flat”. First attested in 1317.
The traditional local form Blåflat developed through assimilation of the initial consonant cluster. Historical sources record the farm and settlement as pronounced Blåflat, while Bruflat is now the usual name of the settlement.
